description: We are a team of undergrad students from the Chittagong University of Engineering & Technology participating in Nasa Space Apps Challenge 2026 for the first time with a shared interest of exploring the outer space & using space data to create solutions for real world problems & limitations. Our skills are- web development, interactive graphics & educative simulations .
summary:
Sol Keeper is a free browser mission trainer where children aged 7 to 12 run a Moon or Mars outpost. A Junior view shows three gauges (Air, Power, Shield) and one decision at a time, while five crew stations, finite crew hours and spare parts work behind them. A Reality Dial shows the same simulation in simple words, real units or full equations, so one tool serves a child, an older sibling and a classroom. Crisis Replays recreate Apollo 13, a 1972 solar storm and the Mir fire.

Every choice shows its price, so nothing is free: saving power slows the garden, and sheltering from a storm costs work time. Real NASA data drives the simulation, including DONKI space weather, JPL Horizons light-time delay, Trek maps and NASA technical documents. Each number has a source and a label, and each external data point is badged Live, Snapshot or Archived. Consoles follow their world: Mars dust storms bury the solar panels, so a cleaning lever exists; the Moon has none. A Black Box debrief replays the chain of decisions behind a result, and a seeded class link gives thirty students the identical mission with no accounts.

Most space content shows mission outcomes, not the decisions behind them. As people return to the Moon and look toward Mars, children who understand trade-offs, evidence and risk are better prepared to follow that work and join it. Sol Keeper teaches that logic honestly, runs offline and collects nothing.
details:
HOW IT WORKS
Sol Keeper is a free, browser-based mission trainer for children aged 7 to 12. A player runs a Moon or Mars outpost day by day: plan, run the day, and answer a Decision Card whenever something needs a call. The Junior view shows three gauges (Air, Power, Shield) and one decision at a time, and every option shows its price in crew hours, power or radiation. Behind the gauges, five stations (Power, Life Support, Communications, Incident Command, Mission Command) are staffed by named crew; a tired or injured crew member makes their station slower and less reliable. Crew hours and spare parts are finite, so no choice is free.

The engine is an hourly physics simulation written in pure TypeScript: sunlight by distance and dust, batteries and a 40 kWe fission reactor, oxygen and CO2 with a cabin-to-inspired-pressure conversion, water recovery, crop growth, heat, radiation dose by location and shielding, and crew health (thirst, hunger, cold, radiation). It uses a seeded random generator, so the same seed and choices always give the same run. Real NASA data feeds it: DONKI space weather can trigger storms, JPL Horizons sets Mission Control’s message delay, Moon and Mars Trek maps help pick landing sites, and NASA documents supply the constants. Every external data point is badged Live, Snapshot or Archived.

A Reality Dial shows the same simulation at three depths: Cadet (plain words and icons), Specialist (real units) and Commander (equations and flow rates). After each mission a Black Box replays the chain of decisions behind the result.

BENEFITS
Children feel a trade-off instead of reading about one: saving power slows the garden, sheltering costs work time, and a repair can use the spare part you needed later. Failure is safe and explained, because the Black Box shows what happened and what to change. Parents and older siblings can go deeper with the dial. Teachers get a free class link: thirty students fly the identical mission, with no accounts, no install and no data collected. The game works offline.

INTENDED IMPACT
We want more children to see that space missions are decisions under limits, and to meet the real constraints NASA planners face: power through a lunar night, radiation during a solar storm, and a message that takes minutes to reach Mars. Because the game is free, accountless and offline-capable, it can reach classrooms with few devices and weak connections, including in Bangladesh. The sources are visible in the game, so students and teachers can check the science themselves.

TOOLS
Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Zustand, i18next, Leaflet and SVG, in a pnpm monorepo with a separate engine package. Testing and quality: Vitest, ESLint, Prettier and Lighthouse. Hosting: Vercel, with TypeScript serverless functions that call the NASA APIs and cache their answers, and a progressive web app for offline play. Data: NASA DONKI, JPL Horizons, the NASA Image and Video Library, Moon and Mars Trek, and NASA technical documents. Development: VS Code, Git and GitHub, and Claude Code, Google Antigravity as an AI coding assistant. Visual elements: custom made UI, gemini omni 1.1 flash for 2D video animations. Hardware: ordinary laptops; players need only a browser. No AI runs in the game.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

  • One simulation, three depths: the Reality Dial changes only the presentation, so one game fits a 7-year-old and a classroom.
  • Consoles follow their world: on Mars, dust storms bury the solar panels, so a cleaning lever appears and costs crew time and radiation. The Moon has no dust storms, so it has none.
  • Crisis Replays: Apollo 13’s carbon dioxide problem, a 1972 solar storm as a what-if, and the 1997 Mir fire, where NASA’s own records give about 90 seconds and 14 minutes. We show both figures.
  • Inspectable evidence: each number has a source and a label (measured, derived, tuned or placeholder), and a Data Passport shows what each dataset drives.
  • A class mission in a URL: because the simulation is deterministic, one link carries the whole mission.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
Accuracy before polish: automated tests reproduce NASA figures and show that doing nothing fails, and practice crews check the balance. Honesty: where a NASA figure does not fit (cold-survival data is for water, not air), we convert it and label it derived, and a known-limitations document lists what is unfinished. Audience: Cadet text is written near a grade-5 reading level, and crew-loss wording is gentle, with no injuries described. Privacy: no accounts, no free text, nothing leaves the device. Access: offline play, a low-power mode, reduced motion, and status never shown by colour alone. Rights: NASA photos carry their credits, we use no NASA logo, and we disclose AI use. Time: we cut features rather than ship anything half-built.
